title: Mediocre arrangements, and Jelly Roll Morton calling tunes by number
summary: Most bands' arrangements he played were lousy but had to be played; he jokes about Jelly Roll Morton's numbered stock tunes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: This is tape number six, with Herman Autrey. We were talking at the end of the last tape about Fats Waller's big band, and the people who wrote the arrangements for it. As I remember, now, that I think of it, Herman, you didn't really think much of most of the arrangements for that band. What was wrong with them?

Well, as I think back, most bands -- I would say most bands, well, the bands that I have been lucky enough to work with, and play with, most of their arrangements were mediocre. I mean lousy, to be frank, brutally frank.
(Laughter.)
And -- but you had to play them anyway. I mean if you want to work, well you play what the man has. You play what's there, you know?
Yeah.
(Laughs.) I can drop a little joke in here right here. Speaking of arrangements, and music, uh, uh, Benny -- not Benny --
Piano ?
Yeah, piano, yeah. Jelly Roll Morton.
Jelly Roll Morton.
Yeah, Gosh, you know he had a nice book of -- well arrangements, stocks, everything that come out. Years ago you could walk downtown, any music stores, and

just ask for some music, and they would give you a bundle. You couldn't get uptown with it. You'd have to tie a string around it to get uptown, and you'd pick out what you wanted, and the rest of it, you threw it away, or give it away, you know.

So he was doing a dance somewhere, in Harlem, or Jersey, or somewhere, Brooklyn, and he always had himself a ten or twelve piece band, you know. They wasn't making any money anyway, but you know, and he'd get his baton, looked like a long broomstick, and he would direct his group.
Oh, he stood up and conducted?
Most times. You know.
Did he sit down and play piano too?
He'd sit down and play piano, yeah.

And anyway, but what I'm trying to get to, as you call out some tune, they played it, and the set went down, the dance, so the guys sat there waiting. So okay, Jelly Johnny, what's next? He say, what you mean, what's next? Well, I mean we just finished playing. What other tunes do you want?
He said well, what did we do? The guys say one, two, three. He says okay, four, five, six.
(Laughter.)

You know. What the heck, he has them all numbered down, but you know how they numbered music, these days, the waltzes was this and that and the other. You coudn't go -- well anyway, you got -- wait and see what he's going to

call. Well that happens in too many bands. The guys want to be kept interesting, you know, say well let's do something interesting to each other, and be nice when you did call out an arrangement that was good. A guy felt like doing it, you say I did it last week, or last month, and I enjoyed playing it, but every night, and when you finish, you say whew! When am I going to leave this band and join a good band, you know? (laughs.)
